title: Son of Man, I Am Sending You
summary: The voice from the throne addresses Ezekiel as son of man and tells him to stand. The Spirit enters him and sets him on his feet. God sends him to the Israelites, a rebellious house, and tells him not to fear them whether they listen or refuse. Then a hand holds out a scroll written on both sides with words of lamentation, mourning, and woe, and God tells Ezekiel to open his mouth and eat what he is given.
story: Chapter 1 ended with Ezekiel face down before the glory of the LORD, hearing a voice. Chapter 2 is what the voice says. The vision now becomes a commission: the priest in exile is made a prophet. The commissioning continues through chapter 3, and together chapters 1 to 3 form the call narrative that opens the book, like the call stories of Moses (Exodus 3 and 4), Isaiah (Isaiah 6), and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1). What stands out here is how bleak the prospect is. Ezekiel is not promised success. He is promised resistance, and told that his task is faithfulness, whether or not anyone listens. The scroll full of lament prepares him, and the reader, for the long message of judgment in chapters 4 to 24.
historical:
The setting is the same as chapter 1: the summer of 593 BC, among the exiles in Babylonia who had been deported with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC. The Israelites to whom Ezekiel is sent (verse 3) are, in the first place, these exiles, although his message also concerns Jerusalem, which was still standing under King Zedekiah. At this time both communities were hearing prophets who promised a quick end to Babylonian domination. Jeremiah, writing to the exiles from Jerusalem at about this time, warned them not to believe such prophets and to settle in for a long stay (Jeremiah 29:1-9, 15-23). Ezekiel's commission places him in the same hard position: sent to people who wanted a different message.

The charge that they and their fathers have rebelled to this very day (verse 3) reflects the prophets' reading of Israel's history as a long pattern of unfaithfulness, from the wilderness to the monarchy. Ezekiel will later retell that history at length (chapters 16, 20, and 23).
cultural:
Scrolls in the ancient Near East were made of papyrus or leather sheets joined into long strips and rolled. Normally they were written only on the inside, where the surface was smoother and protected when rolled. A scroll written on the front and back (verse 10) was unusual; it suggests a message so full that there was no room left, and nothing Ezekiel could add of his own. Words of lamentation, mourning, and woe describe the content: funeral songs and cries of grief, the genres of a coming catastrophe.

Prophesying in the ancient world could be dangerous. Kings and communities often punished messengers whose words they disliked; Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned, and the prophet Uriah was executed by King Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26:20-23). The images of briers, thorns, and scorpions (verse 6) picture an environment that would wound Ezekiel at every step. The command to eat the scroll draws on the idea, found also in Jeremiah 15:16, that a prophet must take God's word into himself before he can speak it; the act itself follows in chapter 3.
literary: The chapter is part of a call narrative and is built mostly of divine speech. It is framed by two actions: the Spirit setting Ezekiel on his feet (verse 2) and the hand offering him the scroll (verses 9 and 10). Repetition carries the message. God addresses Ezekiel as son of man four times in the first eight verses. The word rebellious or rebellion appears again and again: a rebellious nation, a rebellious house, do not be rebellious like that rebellious house. The phrase whether they listen or refuse to listen appears twice (verses 5 and 7) and returns in chapter 3. Three times Ezekiel is told not to be afraid (verse 6). The final command, open your mouth and eat (verse 8), turns the focus from Israel's rebellion to Ezekiel's obedience: the prophet must not be like his hearers.

outline.t: Stand up: the Spirit sets Ezekiel on his feet
Do not be afraid of them
Eat what I give you: the scroll of lament

doctrines.note: “The Spirit entered me and set me on my feet” (verse 2). Ezekiel cannot stand before God or carry out his calling in his own strength. The Spirit's empowering is a thread through the book, climaxing in the promise to put God's Spirit within all his people (36:27).

The prophet speaks only what he is given: “you are to say to them, ‘This is what the Lord GOD says’” (verse 4). The scroll is handed to him already written. His message comes from God, not from his own insight or the audience's wishes.

Israel is described as obstinate, stubborn, and rebellious, and this rebellion runs across generations (verse 3). The chapter treats sin not as isolated acts but as a settled posture of resistance to God.

words.note: Adam, man or humanity. Son of man (ben adam) is Ezekiel's standard title, used for him more than ninety times in the book. It means simply a human being, a mortal, and it stresses the distance between the prophet and the glorious God who addresses him.

Meri, rebellion or rebelliousness. Ezekiel's favorite description of Israel is a house of rebellion (verse 5). The word implies deliberate, bitter opposition. The command in verse 8, do not be rebellious like that rebellious house, shows that the prophet himself is not immune.

Megillah, a scroll. The word is used for rolled documents and later became the Jewish name for the five festival scrolls, including Lamentations. Here the scroll is God's message in written form, full on both sides.

christ: The title son of man is Ezekiel's ordinary name, meaning a mortal, and the New Testament's use of the phrase for Jesus draws mainly on Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man receives an everlasting kingdom. Still, Jesus' use of the title holds both meanings together: he is the heavenly figure of Daniel and also a real human being who, like Ezekiel, was sent to a people who would not listen. Jesus described himself as sent by the Father to speak his words (John 12:49), spoke of prophets being rejected by their own (Luke 4:24), and wept over Jerusalem's refusal (Luke 13:34). He was empowered by the Spirit for his mission (Luke 4:18). Unlike Ezekiel, who is warned not to be rebellious, Jesus was perfectly obedient. The connection is one of pattern: Ezekiel's calling foreshadows the faithful messenger that Christ fully is.

hard.q: Why would God send a prophet to people he knows will not listen?
hard.a: The chapter does not promise that Ezekiel's hearers will repent; it says that whether they listen or not, they will know that a prophet has been among them (verse 5). Some readers find this troubling: what is the point of preaching to people who will refuse? Several answers have been given. First, the message is a witness: it makes God's warning clear, so that judgment, when it comes, cannot be mistaken for chance or for the defeat of Israel's God. Second, the call to faithfulness rather than results protects the messenger from despair and pride alike. Third, the statement is about the nation as a whole, and individuals within it could still respond; chapter 18 and the watchman passages insist that anyone who turns will live. Finally, the book as a whole looks beyond the rebellious generation to a future in which God gives a new heart that will listen (36:26). The refusal of the hearers is not the end of the story.

questions: Ezekiel is told that success is not his measure; faithfulness is. How would it change your work, service, or witness to measure it that way?
God tells Ezekiel three times not to be afraid. What fears keep you from saying or doing what you know is right?
Ezekiel must take in God's word before speaking it. What does it look like for you to take Scripture into yourself rather than only reading about it?
